solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Piece of bread on empty Southport promenade (6)

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is placed after it, so ROLL is sent second, after ST
an emptied word has lost its insides, leaving only its outer letters

annotation.surface: A slice of bread lying on a deserted seafront walk at Southport, the Merseyside resort.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface places the bread on the promenade; in the wordplay the roll goes on (after) ST. Southport is a seaside town in north-west England, fitting the promenade picture.
annotation.definitionFit: A promenade is a leisurely walk, the same as a stroll.

entries.clue: Calm down opponents before meeting? (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first piece comes before (above) the second

blocks.note: South and East, opposing players at the bridge table
a date is an arranged meeting

annotation.surface: Advice to settle your nerves before facing rivals.
annotation.walkthrough: In bridge, South partners North, so East and West are South's opponents; crosswords use any such pair of compass points for 'opponents'.
annotation.definitionFit: To sedate someone is to calm them down, usually with a drug.

entries.clue: Perhaps Tommy Cooper daftly entertaining a thousand? Right answer! (4,5)

indicators.note: done daftly, the letters of COOPER are jumbled
the jumbled letters host K inside them

blocks.note: A = answer, as in Q and A

annotation.surface: The comedian Tommy Cooper fooling about for a crowd of a thousand, with someone crying 'Right answer!'
annotation.walkthrough: Tommy is not the comedian but the Who's 1969 rock opera; 'Perhaps' flags it as an example. K sits inside the jumbled COOPER (ROC-K-OPE), then R and A follow.
annotation.definitionFit: The Who's Tommy is the best-known rock opera.

entries.clue: Hero-worship of big cat is close to insane (7)

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: the lion is a big cat

annotation.surface: A claim that idolising a big cat borders on madness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hero-worship' reads as a noun in the surface, but it is the verb here, matching LIONISE.
annotation.definitionFit: To lionise someone is to treat them as a celebrity, to hero-worship them.

entries.clue: Stands behind counter and jeers (8)

indicators.note: the RACKS piece comes behind, after, the BAR piece

blocks.note: a bar is a counter where drinks are served
racks are stands for holding things

annotation.surface: A barman who stands behind the counter and heckles customers.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Stands' a verb; in the wordplay it is the noun RACKS. To barrack is chiefly British and Australian for jeering at a speaker or player.
annotation.definitionFit: To barrack someone is to jeer at them, so 'barracks' = 'jeers'.

entries.clue: Very old article entertains banker in Bristol (4)

indicators.note: a host entertains guests in the house, so the article takes the other letters inside it

blocks.note: V = very, as in v. good

annotation.surface: An ancient newspaper article that features a Bristol bank manager.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'banker' in crosswords is often a river, something with banks. The Avon flows through Bristol.
annotation.definitionFit: The River Avon runs through Bristol, and a river is something with banks.

entries.clue: Back at home with first of grandchildren getting up (7)

indicators.note: take only the first letter of the next word

annotation.surface: Home again as the eldest grandchild wakes up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pairs 'rearing' with raising children, but the definition is 'getting up', as a horse rears up.
annotation.definitionFit: Rearing means rising up on the hind legs, getting up.

entries.clue: Clubs argue over new trophy (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first pieces sit over the last

blocks.note: to row (rhymes with cow) is to argue

annotation.surface: Football clubs disputing a new cup.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' reads as sports teams, but it is the card suit, giving C.
annotation.definitionFit: A crown is a title or championship won, as in a boxing crown: a trophy.

entries.clue: Cake plate? (4,4)

blocks.note: read as a sponge for tea, meant as a bar of the stuff you lather your hands with
read as crockery for serving, meant as the small tray the bar rests on by the basin

annotation.surface: A plate for serving cake.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark warns of a trick: the cake is a cake of soap, and the plate it sits on is a soap dish.
annotation.definitionFit: Soap comes in cakes, and a soap dish is the small plate that holds one.

entries.clue: Medic‘s entry after checking constant temperature (6)

indicators.note: the door has stopped, held back, C and T inside it

blocks.note: c is the symbol for a constant in physics, as in the speed of light

annotation.surface: A doctor's arrival after taking a patient's steady temperature.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', so 'Medic‘s' is the definition plus a link. 'After checking' reads as time order in the surface, but 'checking' means holding in.
annotation.definitionFit: Medic is the informal word for any medical practitioner, and a doctor is the commonest kind.

entries.clue: Firm about a school bag regularly providing drink (4-4)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, every second one

annotation.surface: A satchel that holds a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay ends in COLA itself, taken from alternate letters of 'school bag'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the fizzy brand is one of countless soft drinks.

entries.clue: Pal holding Guevara’s weapon (7)

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it in your grasp, so the pal's letters close around the revolutionary's

annotation.surface: A friend carrying Che Guevara's gun.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive makes 'weapon' look like Guevara's belonging; the 's only joins wordplay to definition. MA-CHE-TE.
annotation.definitionFit: A machete is a broad heavy knife that can serve as a weapon.

entries.clue: Sultry Romeo bathed in current (8)

indicators.note: R is immersed inside TOPICAL

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A hot Romeo swimming in a sea current.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like a water flow in the surface, but it is the adjective, meaning up to date. T-R-OPICAL.
annotation.definitionFit: Tropical weather is hot and humid, sultry.

entries.clue: Having besieged hotel, live band finally thrown out (6)

indicators.note: BE surrounds INN, as an army besieges a town
the final letter of the next word

annotation.surface: A live band ejected after occupying a hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hotel' is usually the NATO letter H in crosswords; here it is a word for a place to stay. 'Live' reads as a live band, but it is the verb 'to be'.
annotation.definitionFit: Binned means put in the bin, thrown out.

entries.clue: Deduce name originally of Dante work (7)

indicators.note: the origin of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: Working out a name from the original text of Dante.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Originally' applies to 'of' alone, giving O; the surface wants it to modify the whole of Dante's work.
annotation.definitionFit: Inferno is the first part of Dante's Divine Comedy.

entries.clue: Plant trumpeter in front of whistle-blower (8,5)

indicators.note: the first piece goes in front of the second

blocks.note: a grass is British slang for an informer

annotation.surface: Planting a trumpet player in front of a whistle-blower, as if setting a trap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a verb (to put someone in place), but it is the noun. A trumpeter is not a musician but an animal that trumps: the elephant.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this tall African grass, grazed by the animals it is named after, is one kind of plant.

entries.clue: A bra’s lost at sea – am I flapping over it? (9)

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: Someone who has lost a bra overboard asking if they should panic about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a riddle in the bird's voice: flying over the sea, the albatross flaps over 'it'. 'Flapping' in the surface means panicking.
annotation.definitionFit: The albatross is a seabird that flies for long stretches over the open ocean.

entries.clue: Starts to sense City’s unruly crowd in game (8)

indicators.note: take the starting letters of the next words

blocks.note: first letters of SENSE and CITY
a rabble is a disorderly crowd

annotation.surface: Sensing trouble from Manchester City's rowdy fans at a match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'City' is a football club in the surface, not a place; it gives only its C.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the tile-and-board word contest is one of many games.

entries.clue: The Scarlet Bow, weaving book for children! (10,3)

indicators.note: weaving interlaces the letters into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone weaving a red bow, which sounds like a title for a children's book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Weaving' is apt: Charlotte is the spider who weaves her web in E. B. White's novel.
annotation.definitionFit: Charlotte's Web is E. B. White's classic children's novel.

entries.clue: Some circumflex I consider for dictionary (7)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

annotation.surface: Weighing up whether a circumflex accent belongs in the dictionary.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across three words, starting at the end of 'circumflex'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lexicon, from the Greek for 'of words', is the scholarly name for a dictionary, especially of an ancient language.

entries.clue: Sewiously risky bike trick? (7)

blocks.note: read as a misprint, meant as a speaker who turns every R into a W, so that 'really' comes out with a W at the front
a stunt riding along on the back tyre alone

annotation.surface: A lisping warning that a bike stunt is seriously dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sewiously' shows a speaker who turns R into W. Said their way, 'really risky' becomes 'wheelie risky': the trick is riding on the back wheel.
annotation.definitionFit: A wheelie is a bike trick with the front wheel lifted off the ground.

entries.clue: Immature son joins political party members (6)

indicators.note: S is joined on to the end

annotation.surface: A callow son signs up with a political party.
annotation.walkthrough: Greens are members of the Green Party, as found in Britain and elsewhere.
annotation.definitionFit: Environmentalist parties take their name from the colour, and their members are known by it in the plural.

entries.clue: Queen by East Wing (6)

annotation.surface: Directions to a palace: the queen's rooms are by the east wing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like a link word meaning 'next to', but it is the multiplication sign X.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a building extension joined to the main block is called either, the British spelling keeping the final E.

entries.clue: Not a single individual Echo found after midday (2,3)

indicators.note: something found after another thing sits later in the line, so the letter follows the time of day

blocks.note: Echo is E in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Nobody at all turned up after twelve o'clock.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Echo' is a hint that it is the NATO word for E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the pronoun for nobody, phrased the long way round as 'not a single individual'.

entries.clue: Nosy type unsettling social workers? (8)

blocks.note: read as a busybody, meant as an animal with a very long snout
read as upsetting care staff, meant as raiding colonies of social insects that do the work of the nest

annotation.surface: A busybody who disturbs social services staff.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'nosy type' has a long snout, and the 'social workers' are ants, social insects that it raids.
annotation.definitionFit: An anteater has a long nose and feeds on ants, which are social insects.

entries.clue: Maybe Lancaster bomber’s nose turret occasionally failing (4)

indicators.note: the nose is the front, the first letter
every other letter fails to appear

annotation.surface: A Lancaster bomber whose nose gun turret keeps jamming.
annotation.walkthrough: The Lancaster is the WWII bomber in the surface, but 'Maybe' makes it an example: the film star Burt Lancaster.
annotation.definitionFit: Burt Lancaster was a Hollywood actor, so 'Maybe Lancaster' is BURT.

entries.clue: Chef keen to swap starters for Reading party (4,4)

indicators.note: exchange the first letters of the two words

blocks.note: a chef is a cook, and to keen is to wail, to blub
trade the first letters of the two words, C for B

annotation.surface: An eager chef trading his opening dishes for a party in the town of Reading.
annotation.walkthrough: COOK BLUB with C and B exchanged gives BOOK CLUB. 'Keen' means eager in the surface but is the verb 'wail' here; Reading is a town in Berkshire, but here it means reading books.
annotation.definitionFit: A book club is a group that meets to discuss reading, a reading party.

entries.clue: American chappie accommodating student in recess (6)

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to give them room inside, so the student is taken in between the other letters

blocks.note: cove is old British slang for a chap

annotation.surface: A US guy putting up a student in a nook.
annotation.walkthrough: L comes from the learner plates on British cars. It slips between A and COVE: A-L-COVE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name a space set back into a wall, like a nook for a bed or bookshelf.

entries.clue: Tiny tree growing wild for a long time (8)

indicators.note: the letters run wild into a new order

annotation.surface: A sapling left to grow untended for years.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a slow-growing tree; 'for' is only the link to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Strictly it is endless time, but in everyday exaggeration ('I waited an eternity') it means merely a long wait.

entries.clue: Stops Republican abandoning lines? (6)

indicators.note: R abandons, leaves, the word

blocks.note: creases are lines, as on a face

annotation.surface: A Republican quitting the party line, ending his campaign.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lines' suggests party lines or verse; here they are creases, and dropping R leaves CEASES.
annotation.definitionFit: To cease is to stop, so 'ceases' = 'stops'.
